Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *g⁽ʷ⁾eldʰ- Proto-Indo-European *g⁽ʷ⁾l̥dʰ-ró-s Proto-Indo-Iranian *gr̥dʰrás Sanskrit गृध्र॑ (gṛ́dhra) Prakrit गिद्ध (giddha) Northwestern Indo-Aryanbor. Hindi गिद्ध Inherited from Sauraseni Prakrit गिद्ध (giddha) without cluster simplification—compare Punjabi ਗਿੱਧ /گدھ (giddha)—, from Sanskrit गृध्र (gṛdhra). Doublet of गीध (gīdh) and गृध्र (gŕdhra, “vulturine, rapacious”) and related to गीधना (gīdhnā, “to be greedy”). Cognate with Gujarati ગીધ (gīdh), ગીધડું (gīdhḍũ), Marathi गिधाड (gidhāḍ), Nepali गिद्ध (giddha).
Borrowed from Classical Persian دانه (dāna). Compare Bengali দানা (dana), Nepali दाना (dānā), Punjabi ਦਾਣਾ (dāṇā).
Borrowed from Sanskrit दिव्यचक्षु (divyacakṣu). By surface analysis, दिव्य (divya, “divine”) + चक्षु (cakṣu, “eye”).
Borrowed from Classical Persian دِینِی (dīnī). By surface analysis, दीन (dīn) + ई (-ī).

s.g: Peter, foremost among the Twelve Disciples, and later a leading Apostle, in the New Testament.
